title: More Engineering Output: Three Weave Customer Playbooks
summary: See how Bytes AI increased output 30% in six weeks, OpenZeppelin caught a costly bottleneck, and Intellistack scaled AI adoption with Weave.
body_markdown:
Bytes AI increased engineering output by about 30% in six weeks after giving every engineer access to their Weave profile. The change was practical: engineers could see their own progress, and leadership could use the same data to improve the way the team worked.


That is the standard an engineering intelligence platform should meet. It should help you see what your team produces, understand what affects delivery, and make a better operating decision.


The published experiences of Bytes AI, OpenZeppelin and Intellistack show how to do this with Weave.


**TL;DR**


- Make output visible to the engineers doing the work.
- Review output, quality and delivery together, then investigate the project behind a change.
- Use AI adoption data to focus training and check how output moves afterward.


## 1. Make output visible: the Bytes AI playbook


**The result: 30% more output in six weeks.**


Bytes AI CTO Muthana Alhadrab wanted to understand engineering trends. Management reviewed code, but had no consistent view of how output changed over time. “We were just not seeing any actual trends,” he explained.


Weave initially supported management's one-on-ones. Muthana then opened profiles to the whole engineering team. Engineers could see their output, badges and ranking. Six weeks later, output was up about 30% across the team.


Muthana also used Weave's timetable to investigate weekly dips. Visibility gave him a place to start a useful conversation about the work, time and attention behind the result.


**Put it into practice:**


1. Give engineers access to their own output history.
2. Use the same view in one-on-ones, so progress is visible to both sides.
3. When output changes, inspect the underlying work and activity before choosing an intervention.


This is a useful starting point when the team is already using AI and leadership needs a shared view of what that work produces.


[Read the Bytes AI case](https://weaveos.com/blog/how-bytes-ai-lifted-engineering-output-30-by-making-every-engineers-weave-profile-visible) , by Brennan Lupyrypa.


## 2. Find the bottleneck early: the OpenZeppelin playbook


**The result, in Daniel Carmo's words:**


> It probably saved us 4 weeks of engineering time.


Daniel Carmo, Director of Libraries & Tooling at OpenZeppelin, organized the team's approach around four metrics: average output per engineer, code turnover, PR cycle time and bug ratio. Team data was reviewed weekly, and managers used the dashboards to identify specific actions.


When one project's output was much lower than expected, the team investigated. Weave surfaced a problem early enough for them to act before it became a larger issue.


The operating advantage is the connection between a signal and a decision. A lower-output project becomes something to investigate. Turnover, bug ratio and cycle time give the team more context for deciding what to change.


**Put it into practice:**


1. Review output and the quality and delivery metrics beside it.
2. Choose the project or workflow that needs attention.
3. Record an action and revisit it in the next weekly review.


Use this approach when more activity is not resolving a delivery problem, or when leaders need to locate a bottleneck before it spreads.


[Read the OpenZeppelin case](https://weaveos.com/blog/from-blind-spots-to-bottleneck-detection-how-openzeppelin-saved-four-weeks-of-engineering-time-with-weave) , by Brennan Lupyrypa.


## 3. Focus AI training: the Intellistack playbook


**The result: stronger AI adoption, dramatically higher output over seven months, and hours of monthly manual reporting eliminated.**


Intellistack brought code output and AI usage into one view with Weave. Component-level data showed that backend teams were making strong gains while frontend teams needed more support. That gave leadership a specific place to focus its adoption work.


After training on practices such as Cursor plan mode and automated test writing, leaders could check whether engineers were using those practices and how adoption correlated with output improvements. The same data supported board reporting without repeated exports and spreadsheet work.


Chris Weber, Engineering Director at Intellistack, described the management approach:


> We use it as a way to help drive adoption; it’s an invitation to become curious, you can determine if some people need more training or encouragement for greater AI adoption.


**Put it into practice:**


1. Compare adoption and output by team or component.
2. Choose a training practice that addresses the gap you can see.
3. Review adoption and output together, then bring the findings into the next management discussion.


[Read the Intellistack case](https://weaveos.com/blog/intellistack-scaling-ai-adoption-with-engineering-intelligence) , by Brennan Lupyrypa.

When evaluating engineering intelligence, test it against real management jobs:


- Can you inspect the PR behind an output score?
- Can you compare AI adoption and output across teams or components?
- Can you review output alongside turnover, bug ratio and cycle time?
- Can you use that evidence in a one-on-one, weekly review or board discussion?
